Water on Earth is always moving in an endless journey called the water cycle. The sun is the engine that powers this cycle. Its heat warms oceans, lakes, and rivers, turning water into invisible water vapour — this is evaporation. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves, a process called transpiration. A single large tree can release over 400 litres of water on a hot day.

As warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much vapour, so the vapour turns back into tiny liquid droplets — this is condensation, and it forms clouds. You can see condensation at home when water drops appear on a cold glass.

When cloud droplets join together and grow heavy, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail — all forms of precipitation. India receives most of its rain during the monsoon, from June to September.

Rainwater flows over land into streams and rivers, eventually reaching the sea. Some soaks into the soil and becomes groundwater, which can stay underground for thousands of years. Wells and hand pumps draw on this groundwater, so protecting it from pollution is vital.

The water cycle gives us fresh water for drinking, growing crops, and running industries. It also moves heat around the planet and shapes our weather. Cutting forests, paving over soil, and polluting rivers all disturb this cycle.

arguments.content:
The Water Cycle — A Two-Minute Summary

Water on Earth is always moving in an endless journey called the water cycle. The sun is the engine that powers this cycle. Its heat warms oceans, lakes, and rivers, turning water into invisible water vapour — this is evaporation. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves, a process called transpiration. A single large tree can release over 400 litres of water on a hot day.

As warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much vapour, so the vapour turns back into tiny liquid droplets — this is condensation, and it forms clouds. You can see condensation at home when water drops appear on a cold glass.

When cloud droplets join together and grow heavy, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail — all forms of precipitation. India receives most of its rain during the monsoon, from June to September.

Rainwater flows over land into streams and rivers, eventually reaching the sea. Some soaks into the soil and becomes groundwater, which can stay underground for thousands of years. Wells and hand pumps draw on this groundwater, so protecting it from pollution is vital.

The water cycle gives us fresh water for drinking, growing crops, and running industries. It also moves heat around the planet and shapes our weather. Cutting forests, paving over soil, and polluting rivers all disturb this cycle.

We can help save water with simple habits: turn off the tap while brushing, fix leaks, and collect rainwater from rooftops. A dripping tap can waste 20 litres of water a day. Every drop counts in keeping the water cycle healthy for all of us.
